name: Eito
sub-heading: Lead AI/Data Engineer based in Tokyo.
more-info: I architect and deploy advanced AI systems — from multi-agent LLM platforms and RAG pipelines to production-grade MLOps infrastructure. With 6+ years of experience, I help Fortune 500 companies and scale-ups turn cutting-edge AI into reliable, scalable products.
about-text-top: Hi! I'm Eito, a Lead AI/Data Engineer with over six years of experience building AI systems across enterprise data science, automation, and intelligent agent platforms. I've evolved from traditional machine learning and data analytics to cutting-edge LLM-based architectures, specializing in Generative AI, MLOps, and scalable backend infrastructure.
about-text-bottom: I've delivered production-grade AI solutions that transformed business operations for Fortune 500 companies and scale-ups, with deep expertise in backend development using Python and modern cloud technologies. I'm driven by turning complex requirements into elegant, dependable systems that create real business value.

experience.description: As Engineering Lead at LumoraTech, an AI-focused engineering studio in Edogawa, Tokyo, I lead the team that designs and ships AI systems built to survive production. That means retrieval pipelines with eval-gated deployments, multi-agent architectures on LangGraph, and the full-stack products and data platforms that surround them — delivered remotely, in Japanese or English, for founders and product teams here and abroad.

As Lead AI/Data Engineer at Foundation EGI, I architected multi-agent LLM systems with LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen to automate finance, HR, and operations workflows — cutting operational costs by 35% for Fortune 500 clients. I built RAG pipelines (LlamaIndex, Pinecone, Weaviate) reaching 92% semantic-search accuracy across 10M+ documents, and ran the MLOps and FastAPI microservices that handle 8M+ daily automation requests at 99.9% uptime.

As Senior AI Engineer at Tenchijin, I produced intelligent document-understanding systems with BERT, RoBERTa, and LayoutLM at 94% extraction accuracy, processing 500K+ documents monthly. I built multi-language NLP pipelines across four languages, shipped recommendation engines that lifted conversion by 28%, and pioneered MLOps practices (MLflow, DVC, Kubeflow) that cut time-to-production by 60%.

As a Machine Learning Engineer at Citadel AI, I delivered computer-vision inspection systems (ResNet, EfficientNet, YOLO) at 96% detection accuracy, built predictive-analytics models (XGBoost, LightGBM) that reduced inventory costs by $800K annually, and established Docker/Kubernetes CI/CD pipelines that cut deployment time by 70%.

posts.title: Same Skills, Different Zip Code
posts.excerpt: A Christmas story that actually happened to me this year. I was leading a team at a US company, and on billing day I found that the lead developer in Tokyo was billed less than the junior developer in California. I asked the billing manager to account for my lead role, and got a raise — which brought me level with the junior. Then the math hit me: two of me still equalled one senior US dev. Same skills, same work, different geography. Ah, zip code.
posts.imageAlt: An eight-panel comic. A Japanese developer leads a US-based team in California. On billing day the rates appear: senior US developer $80/hr, junior US developer $50/hr, and the Japan lead developer 5,000 yen, about $40/hr. He asks the billing manager to consider his lead role and is offered $50/hr on the next billing day. The reality panel shows Japan lead developer below junior US developer, then equal to them at maximum, and two Japan lead developers equal to one senior US developer. He wonders why, and the answer is the zip code: same skills, different zip code. He daydreams about being a US-based lead developer at $150/hr, and closes with a handshake captioned partnership over location.

body.text: Konbanwa, friends! Merry Christmas! 🎄
Wishing you a joyful holiday filled with rest and good moments with loved ones.
This story actually happened to me this year, and I hope your holiday is as interesting as this tale.
One day, I found myself leading a team at a US company — two American developers (one senior, one junior) and a few Japanese colleagues, myself included.
Then came billing day. The numbers appeared on the screen:
I stared at the screen. Wait... I'm the lead. How does this make sense?
Frustrated, I walked over to the billing manager.

body.speaker: Me
body.text: Could you at least consider that I'm in a lead role?
Weeks passed. The next billing cycle arrived. The manager approached me with a smile.

body.speaker: Manager
body.text: Hey! How about $50/hr?

body.speaker: Me
body.text: Wow... thanks so much!
I smiled. But then the math hit me.

items: Japan Lead Dev < Junior US Dev (before)
Japan Lead Dev = Junior US Dev (my maximum)
2× Japan Lead Dev = 1× Senior US Dev

body.text: I sat alone that night, asking myself one question:
Why?
And the answer was painfully simple: Ah, zip code.
Same skills. Same work. Different geography.
I caught myself daydreaming...
What if I were a US-based Lead Dev? $150/hr... The thought lingered...
— END —

posts.title: Zero Reviews to Top 3% in Ten Weeks
posts.excerpt: Upwork is the largest freelancing platform in the world, most of its clients are American, and the US market pays the highest rates you will find anywhere. In September 2025 I opened an Upwork account with zero reviews and zero history. One month later my first contract closed at 5.0 stars and about $5K. Ten weeks in, Upwork gave me Top Rated Plus — the top 3% of the platform. This is the method behind it: find the client before you write the proposal, write about their problem instead of your résumé, and stop trying to win a bidding war against somebody who will always spend one more connect than you.
posts.imageAlt: A screenshot of the author's Upwork profile, from the top of the page down through the Portfolio and Education sections. The header shows the name Eito S., a location of Tokyo, Japan, a 100% Job Success score and a Top Rated Plus badge, above a statistics row reading $10K+ total earnings, 5 total jobs and 256 total hours. The left column lists availability, languages, verifications and two degrees, from the University of Tokyo and the Tokyo Institute of Technology. The right column carries the headline Lead AI/Data Engineer, Full-Stack Developer, AI Agent and Agentic AI at $40.00 per hour, a professional overview, and a portfolio of three published projects.

body.text: In September 2025 I opened an Upwork account with zero reviews, zero history and zero ratings. Ten weeks later the platform put me in the top 3% of its talent.

My first contract closed inside a month at 5.0 stars and about $5K. Two and a half months in, Upwork handed me the pink badge: Top Rated Plus, top 3% of talent, $10K+ earned. The Job Success score has stayed at 100% since.

A word on why Upwork and not somewhere else. It is the largest freelancing platform in the world, and that scale is the whole argument. Most of the clients on it are American, and the US market pays the highest rates you will find anywhere — so the biggest pool of work also happens to be the best paid pool of work.

Naturally, I am not the only one who noticed. Every one of those clients is being pitched by freelancers from every continent at once. Being good at the job was never going to be the hard part. Being seen was.
People keep asking how a brand new profile gets past that, usually while assuming I got lucky. So here is the actual method, without the motivational poster version.

Right client, before anything else. Most people treat Upwork like a lottery — fire off forty proposals and hope one lands. I treated it like sales. I find the client on LinkedIn first, read what the company actually ships, who they serve, and where their stack is probably hurting. Only then do I open the proposal box.

Right message. The proposal is about their problem, written in their industry's vocabulary. It is not about my résumé. My résumé is one click away, and they will read it after they have decided I understood them.
The first time I did this, the result was almost funny. The client had exactly one candidate in the pipeline.

body.speaker: Client
body.text: You're the only one I'm interviewing.
One conversation later, I started that week.

Right time. Now the part nobody warns you about. Upwork sells visibility: you spend connects to push your proposal up the client's list, and 300 connects runs about $50. I assumed that would be enough to be seen.
It is not. Because the person beside you bid 301. And the person beside them bid 302. And somebody with more budget than patience bid 303.
It is an auction where the prize is being looked at.

So I stopped trying to outspend people and started trying to out-time them. When you bid matters more than how much you burn. Get in while the job is fresh and the client is still actively reading, and you never have to win the bidding war at all — you only have to be near the top of a page that is still being read.

items: Right client — researched on LinkedIn before I ever open the proposal box
Right message — their industry, their problem, their words
Right time — early, while the client is still reading

body.text: That is the entire system. It fits on a napkin, and it took me from zero to the top 3% in about ten weeks.

I am not going to be modest about this one. Millions of people freelance on Upwork, and Top Rated Plus is the top 3% of them. I got there in ten weeks from a profile with nothing on it — no reviews to trade on, no history to point at, no agency behind me. Five contracts, 256 hours, five-star reviews across the board, and a Job Success score that has not moved off 100%.

body.alt: A screenshot of the Work history section of the same Upwork profile, showing four completed jobs, each rated 5.0 out of 5: a senior full-stack developer role at $1,000, an OpenAI Agent Builder and ChatKit server-side build at $2,045, frontend API integrations for automated blog posts at $2,400, and data pipeline and analytics dashboard engineering at $4,800, each with an excerpt from the client's written feedback.

body.text: Luck does not repeat five times in a row.

Every one of those contracts was real engineering work — data pipelines, agent systems, dashboards that had to keep running long after I logged off. The perfect scores are not for being easy to work with. They are for delivering things that held up.
Five contracts. Five perfect scores. Ten weeks. Bring me the sixth.
— END —
